design_principles.pdf_approach: Shows static lists of outcomes and manually calculated tables.
design_principles.app_approach: Students generate outcomes through 3D interactive sandboxes (coins/dice) before formalizing them.

design_principles.pdf_approach: Defines sets using algebraic notation and text descriptions.
design_principles.app_approach: Uses interactive Venn diagrams and drag-and-drop set builders to physically group outcomes into events.

design_principles.pdf_approach: Presents multi-step formulas (Conditional Probability, Bayes-lite) as full slides.
design_principles.app_approach: Breaks complex problems into sequential interactions: build the sample space, highlight the condition, then calculate.

refinement_changelog.detail: Changed from basic list generation to a clever prediction problem ('How many outcomes for 3 coins?') to build intuition before brute-forcing.
Added 'InteractiveVennSelector' so students can physically click regions of a Venn diagram to answer the AND/OR event logic problem, rather than just text.
Inserted a 'Spot the Mistake' checkpoint for the Never Fail Method. Instead of just doing drills, students must debug a pre-filled table, building deeper mastery.
Upgraded the Addition Rule problem to feature a 'Double Count' trap visual that glows red when they forget to subtract the intersection.
Added a 'Probability Matrix Grid' to visually prove independence (showing area = width * height), moving away from pure algebra.
Added a final stretch problem for sampling without replacement (3 consecutive draws) to synthesize conditional probability and trees.

refinement_summary: Pass 2 transformed static questions into highly visual, manipulative exercises. By adding interactive Venn selectors, a 'Spot the Mistake' debugging exercise, and visual proofs for independence, the lecture now prioritizes intuition over rote memorization. The pacing was also improved with a mid-lecture debugging checkpoint and a final stretch synthesis problem.

slides.title: Why Probability?
slides.content_summary: Introduction to probability theory as the science of uncertainty. Real-world examples (elections, finance, medicine, sports) show how we model the unknown.
slides.interactivity: Tap cards to flip them and reveal the hidden 'probability' behind real-world uncertainties.

visual_spec.student_actions: Taps on cards labeled 'Elections', 'Crypto', 'Medical Test', 'UFC' to reveal the core probability question behind each.
visual_spec.implementation: React grid with CSS flip animations and a dynamic 'odds' counter that updates rapidly before settling.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Motivates the study of probability for decision-making under uncertainty.

slides.lux_integration: Lux greets the student: 'We can't predict the future, but we can measure the exact shape of our uncertainty. Let's look at the dice.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Introduce probability not as math, but as a superpower for predicting real-world outcomes.

slides.title: What is an Experiment?
slides.content_summary: Defines probability experiments and outcomes. Highlights that outcomes must be mutually exclusive and at the 'finest grain'.
slides.interactivity: Tap to simulate a coin toss and see the branching outcomes physically log on screen.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click 'Toss Coin' to watch a 3D coin land on Heads or Tails, registering the outcome in an ongoing timeline log.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Grounds the abstract definition of an 'experiment' in physical reality.

slides.lux_integration: Lux points out that 'finest grain' means we cannot break the outcome down any further. 'A coin can't be mostly heads.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Ensure student understands 'mutually exclusive' (cannot be both H and T at the same time).

slides.title: Predicting Outcomes: Multiple Coins
slides.content_summary: Applies the definition to a multi-coin toss, asking the student to predict total unique outcomes before listing them.
slides.interactivity: Problem check.

visual_spec.student_actions: After guessing the number, a branching tree of dots unfurls to visually prove the 2^N growth of outcomes.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Builds intuition for permutations and the size of a sample space.

problem_spec.prompt: If we toss THREE distinct coins (Coin 1, 2, and 3), how many total fine-grained outcomes exist? (Hint: Order matters. HHT is different from HTH).

slides.lux_integration: If student inputs 6 (3*2) or 4 (H, T, HT, etc.), Lux gives a hint: 'Try drawing a tree. The first coin has 2 paths. From each of those, the second coin has 2 paths...'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Distinguish between combinations and permutations intuitively here.

slides.title: Defining the Sample Space
slides.content_summary: Introduces the sample space (S) as the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
slides.interactivity: Hover over mathematical notation to reveal plain-English definitions.

visual_spec.student_actions: Hovering over script S, curly braces {}, and lowercase o reveals interactive tooltips describing the Master Set and Individual Elements.
visual_spec.implementation: React DOM with Framer Motion hover states.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Teaches proper mathematical notation without overwhelming text walls.

slides.lux_integration: Lux clarifies that curly braces {} literally mean 'a collection of'.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Focus on the transition from conceptual list to formal mathematical set.

slides.title: Build the Sample Space
slides.content_summary: Practice formally writing out the sample space for the two-coin experiment.
slides.interactivity: Drag and drop outcomes into the set bracket.

visual_spec.student_actions: Drag visual outcome chips (H1H2, H1T2, T1H2, T1T2) into a pulsing bounding box marked S = { }. Chips snap into place.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Reinforces that S is a collection of specific outcome elements.

problem_spec.prompt: Construct the Sample Space S for a two-coin toss by dragging all valid outcomes into the set brackets.

slides.lux_integration: When the set is complete, Lux celebrates: 'Perfect! That is the entire universe of possibilities for this experiment.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Provide immediate visual validation when a set is complete.

slides.title: Events are Subsets
slides.content_summary: Defines an Event as a subset of outcomes. Shows how to extract outcomes that meet a specific logical condition.
slides.interactivity: Toggle conditions to see which outcomes in the sample space light up.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click chips labeled 'At least one Heads', 'Second coin is Heads'. The corresponding set elements illuminate with a neon outline.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Visually connects plain English conditions to mathematical subsets.

slides.lux_integration: Lux emphasizes that an event is just a 'bucket' we put specific outcomes into based on a rule.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Define event formally but explain intuitively.

slides.title: Combining Events (AND / OR)
slides.content_summary: Introduces set operations. AND creates an intersection, OR creates a union.
slides.interactivity: Manipulate a Venn diagram to observe intersections and unions.

visual_spec.student_actions: Hover over 'A AND B' vs 'A OR B' text to see the intersection or total area glow on the Venn SVG. The outcome list below updates dynamically.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Shows the mechanical outcome of set logic operators visually.

slides.lux_integration: Lux reminds the student that OR is inclusive in math—it means A, B, or BOTH.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Ensure OR is explicitly defined as inclusive.

slides.title: Practice: Event Logic
slides.content_summary: Students must identify the outcomes in a combined event using AND/OR logic.
slides.interactivity: Click regions of a Venn diagram to select the outcomes.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click the distinct zones of the Venn diagram (A-only, overlap, B-only, outside) to answer the prompt.
visual_spec.implementation: Interactive SVG with clickable path elements.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Connects spatial reasoning to algebraic set notation.

problem_spec.prompt: If Event A is 'First coin is Heads' and Event B is 'At least one Tails', click the region representing (A AND B). Which outcome lives there?

slides.lux_integration: If they click the union (entire circles), Lux says: 'That's A OR B! We want A AND B—where do the two circles overlap?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Step-by-step guidance on intersection.

slides.title: The Probability Number
slides.content_summary: Defines probability as a number between 0 and 1. Explains the additive property: P(A) is the sum of probabilities of its outcomes.
slides.interactivity: Slide a bar from 0 (Impossible) to 1 (Certain) to see example events populate.

visual_spec.student_actions: Drag a slider. At 0, shows 'Rolling a 7 on a 6-sided die'. At 0.5, shows 'Flipping Heads'. At 1, shows 'Flipping Heads or Tails'.
visual_spec.implementation: HTML Range Input with dynamic labels.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Establishes the absolute bounds of probability and P(S) = 1.

slides.lux_integration: Lux notes that if probabilities of a sample space sum to anything other than 1, you've missed an outcome or miscalculated.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Focus on the axiom P(S) = 1.

slides.title: Symmetry and Summation
slides.content_summary: Demonstrates calculating P(A) for 'at least one head' by summing equally likely outcomes (1/4 each).
slides.interactivity: Click outcomes to 'add' them to the probability total.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click H1H2, H1T2, T1H2. As each is clicked, an equation physically builds: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. A pie chart fills up.
visual_spec.implementation: React dynamic equation builder and SVG pie chart.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Visualizes the additive property of probability for mutually exclusive outcomes.

slides.lux_integration: Lux validates that 'symmetry' means a fair coin makes all specific fine-grained outcomes equally likely.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Define symmetry clearly as it applies to fair experiments.

slides.title: Calculate P(A)
slides.content_summary: Calculate the exact probability of a specific event using summation.
slides.interactivity: Input a fraction.

visual_spec.student_actions: As the student types their numerator, the corresponding number of outcomes glow in the visual grid.
visual_spec.implementation: React state bound to input value.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Ties the abstract fraction to the physical count of outcomes.

problem_spec.prompt: What is the probability of the event 'Exactly one head occurs' in a two-coin toss?

slides.lux_integration: Lux asks: 'Which specific outcomes give you exactly one head? How many are there out of the total 4?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Guide student to count target outcomes and divide by total outcomes.

slides.title: A Systematic Approach
slides.content_summary: Introduces the 4-step Never Fail Method: Set up sample space, assign probabilities, identify outcomes for the event, add them up.
slides.interactivity: Step through a dice roll example.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click 'Next Step' to watch a table automatically populate with outcomes (1-6), probabilities (1/6), and checkmarks for Event A (At least 4).
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Models the exact tabular approach from the PDF.

slides.lux_integration: Lux explains: 'It seems slow, but this table guarantees you won't make a mistake on tricky overlap questions.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Emphasize reliability of the method over speed.

slides.title: Spot the Mistake!
slides.content_summary: A clever problem to ensure they understand the logic, not just the rote steps. A pre-filled table has one fatal error.
slides.interactivity: Click the incorrect cell in the table.

visual_spec.student_actions: Hover over cells. Click to flag the 'bug'.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Forces critical evaluation of set intersections and complements.

problem_spec.prompt: Someone used the Never Fail Method to find P(Even OR >4) on a die roll, but they got 5/6. Click the cell where they made a mistake checking an outcome.
problem_spec.correct_answer_form: Click the checkmark on outcome '5' under the 'Even' column (or similar manufactured error).

slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Wait, look at row 5. Is 5 an even number? Check your ANDs and ORs carefully!'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Focus on debugging to build deeper mastery of the method.

slides.title: Apply the Never Fail Method
slides.content_summary: Students fill out a mini Never Fail table from scratch to solve a combined event problem.
slides.interactivity: Check boxes in a table and calculate the final sum.

visual_spec.student_actions: Check boxes in a column for 'Event: Even AND > 3', then enter the final fraction.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Forces the student to execute the steps they just learned.

problem_spec.prompt: Roll a fair die. Let A = 'even number' and B = 'greater than 3'. Check the outcomes that belong to (A AND B), then enter the final probability.

slides.lux_integration: If the sum is wrong but checkboxes are right, Lux prompts: 'You found the correct outcomes! Now just add up their probabilities (1/6 each).'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Scaffold: Check outcomes first, then verify the math.

slides.title: The Complement Rule (NOT)
slides.content_summary: Introduces the rule P(NOT A) = 1 - P(A). Shows how finding the probability of what you *don't* want is sometimes easier.
slides.interactivity: Toggle between calculating 'at least one head' directly vs calculating 'no heads' and subtracting from 1.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click to toggle view. A horizontal bar representing '1' splits into P(A) [75%] and P(not A) [25%]. They perfectly tile the 100% space.
visual_spec.implementation: CSS Flexbox with percentage widths and transitions.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Visually proves that an event and its complement perfectly make up the whole sample space.

slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Whenever you see 'at least one', always think of the NOT rule. What is the opposite of at least one?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Highlight 'at least one' as a major keyword for the complement rule.

slides.title: The Addition Rule (Don't Double Count!)
slides.content_summary: Practice calculating P(A OR B) using the formula P(A) + P(B) - P(A AND B) to avoid double counting.
slides.interactivity: Calculate and enter the probability.

visual_spec.student_actions: If a student inputs an answer that implies double counting (e.g., adding P(A) and P(B) directly), the intersection of the Venn diagram flashes red and buzzes.
visual_spec.implementation: SVG with keyframe animations triggered by specific incorrect input states.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Visually reinforces the subtraction of the intersection in the formula.

problem_spec.when_to_place: After introducing the OR rule formula.
problem_spec.prompt: Roll a fair die. A = 'Even number', B = 'Less than 4'. Find P(A OR B).

slides.lux_integration: If student answers 5/6, Lux says: 'You added P(Even) and P(<4), but what about the number 2? You counted it twice! Subtract the overlap.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Catch double-counting errors immediately.

slides.title: Updating with New Information
slides.content_summary: Introduces Conditional Probability. Shows how a prior baseline forecast is adjusted when a new condition (clouds) is known.
slides.interactivity: Slide to reveal 'new information' and watch the probability shift.

visual_spec.student_actions: Drag a slider labeled 'Look out the window (See Clouds)'. The displayed probability of rain dynamically shifts from 20% to 80% with an animated gauge.
visual_spec.implementation: React state update with D3/SVG gauge animation.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Demonstrates the conceptual shift from unconditional to conditional probability.

slides.lux_integration: Lux introduces the vertical bar notation '|', reading it as 'given that'.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Anchor notation to plain English immediately.

slides.title: The Conditional Formula
slides.content_summary: Presents P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Visually explains how the condition 'shrinks' the sample space.
slides.interactivity: Apply a condition to a sample space to watch the irrelevant outcomes fade out.

visual_spec.student_actions: View 6 dice outcomes. Click 'Given it is EVEN'. The odd outcomes physically dissolve. The remaining 3 outcomes visually snap together to become the new denominator.
visual_spec.implementation: React grid with Framer Motion layout transitions.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Shows physically why P(B) becomes the new denominator.

slides.lux_integration: Lux points out: 'The new 'universe' of possibilities is just the condition B. Everything outside of B is now impossible.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Emphasize the shrinking sample space concept.

slides.title: Calculate Conditional Probability
slides.content_summary: Calculate P(A|B) using the formula and values derived from the Never Fail method.
slides.interactivity: Problem check.

problem_spec.prompt: Roll a fair die. Event A is 'at least 4'. Event B is 'the die is even'. What is P(A|B)?

slides.lux_integration: If incorrect, Lux asks: 'First, what is P(B)? Now, what is P(A and B)? Divide the overlap by the new total.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Walk through the numerator and denominator separately.

slides.title: Independence
slides.content_summary: Defines independence intuitively (knowing B tells you nothing about A) and mathematically (P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) and P(A|B) = P(A)).
slides.interactivity: Compare two scenarios: coin flips vs drawing cards without replacement.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click 'Flip a Coin Twice' vs 'Draw Two Cards'. Sees a live probability tree update to show one set of branches is constant, while the other changes based on the first draw.
visual_spec.implementation: React two-column layout with dynamic data.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Contrasts independent vs dependent events clearly.

slides.lux_integration: Lux points out that 'independence' is a specific mathematical property, not just a feeling.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Define mathematical independence strictly.

slides.title: Visualizing Independence
slides.content_summary: A geometric proof of independence. Shows that P(A and B) is literally the area of a rectangle formed by P(A) width and P(B) height.
slides.interactivity: Drag event bounds to see if the intersection area matches the product of the sides.

visual_spec.student_actions: Drag grid lines representing P(A) and P(B). If the events are independent, the overlapping block perfectly matches the mathematical product area.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Connects the algebraic rule P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) to geometric intuition.

slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Think of independence like a perfect rectangle. If P(A and B) doesn't perfectly match the width times the height, they are dependent.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Use area models to explain probability multiplication.

slides.title: Testing for Independence
slides.content_summary: Test if two events are independent using the multiplication rule.
slides.interactivity: Select Yes/No and calculate the product.

problem_spec.when_to_place: Following the mathematical definition and visual proof.
problem_spec.prompt: Roll a die. A = 'Even', B = 'Greater than 4'. Are A and B independent? (Hint: Does P(A and B) equal P(A) * P(B)?)
inputs: fraction input for P(A and B)

slides.lux_integration: Lux guides the proof: 'Let's check the math. What is P(A)*P(B)? Now, look at our sample space. What is the actual P(A and B)? Do they match?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Require mathematical proof for independence, not just intuition.

slides.title: Mapping Sequences: Probability Trees
slides.content_summary: Introduces probability trees for multi-stage experiments. Explains nodes, branches, leaves, and the multiplication rule along paths.
slides.interactivity: Trace a path to see the multiplication happen automatically.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click nodes left to right to build a path. The app highlights the path in gold and displays the multiplied probability formula at the leaf.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Teaches the fundamental rule that probabilities along branches are multiplied.

slides.lux_integration: Lux emphasizes that second-level branches are ALWAYS conditional probabilities based on the first branch.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Drill path multiplication.

slides.title: Build a Tree: Fair & Unfair Coins
slides.content_summary: Construct a tree for an experiment with a fair coin, followed by an unfair coin (if H) or a fair coin (if T).
slides.interactivity: Fill in the missing probabilities on the branches.

visual_spec.student_actions: Type fractions into empty boxes located on the branches of a 2-stage tree.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Validates understanding of conditional assignment on tree branches.

problem_spec.when_to_place: After introducing the rules of trees.
problem_spec.prompt: You toss a fair coin. If Heads, you toss an unfair coin (P(H)=1/3). If Tails, you toss a fair coin again. Fill in the probabilities for the second set of branches.

slides.lux_integration: If an input is wrong, Lux hints: 'Remember, branches leaving a single node must add up to 1 (100% of possibilities).'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Check that sub-branches sum to 1.

slides.title: Calculating from the Tree
slides.content_summary: Use the completed tree to calculate a complex conditional probability (Bayes-lite logic).
slides.interactivity: Problem check with a static completed tree visible.

visual_spec.student_actions: Student can click leaves to highlight the relevant paths for their scratchpad calculation. Calculates path products automatically.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Synthesizes trees and conditional probability formulas.

problem_spec.prompt: Using your tree, what is the probability the first toss was heads, given that the two tosses resulted in different faces?

slides.lux_integration: Lux breaks it down: 'Step 1: Find P(different faces). Which paths give different faces? Add them up. Step 2: Which of those paths started with Heads?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Guide through Bayes theorem logic without explicitly naming it yet.

slides.title: The Changing Sample Space
slides.content_summary: Introduces the Colored Balls problem. Visualizes how drawing without replacement fundamentally alters the sample space for the next draw.
slides.interactivity: Draw a ball from an urn and watch the total counts update.

visual_spec.student_actions: Click to draw a blue ball from an urn containing 2 Blue, 2 Red. The ball physically exits. The denominator for the next draw updates to /3.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Makes the abstract concept of 'without replacement' tangible.

slides.lux_integration: Lux points out that this is conditional probability in physical form: the second draw depends entirely on the first.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Connect 'without replacement' to dependent events.

slides.title: Calculate Conditional Urn Probability
slides.content_summary: Calculate P(2nd Blue | 1st Blue).
slides.interactivity: Solve the problem.

visual_spec.student_actions: Provides a visual aid where they can 'test' drawing the first ball before answering.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Validates the tree math with a physical count.

problem_spec.prompt: An urn has 2 Blue balls and 2 Red balls. What is the probability of drawing a 2nd Blue ball given that the 1st ball drawn was Blue (and not replaced)?
params_for_regenerate: starting counts of blue and red balls

slides.lux_integration: If the student struggles, Lux asks: 'After taking out one Blue ball, how many balls are left in total? How many of those are Blue?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Urge the intuitive physical counting method as a verification of the math formula.

slides.title: Synthesis: 3 Draws
slides.content_summary: A final synthesis problem challenging students to calculate the probability of a specific 3-draw sequence without replacement.
slides.interactivity: Calculate a 3-part multiplied fraction.

visual_spec.student_actions: A 3-stage tree that is mostly empty, prompting them to visualize the changing probabilities.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Combines multiplication rules with changing sample spaces.

problem_spec.when_to_place: Final challenge slide of the lecture.
problem_spec.prompt: An urn has 3 Blue balls and 2 Red balls. If you draw 3 balls without replacement, what is the exact probability of drawing Blue, then Red, then Blue in that specific order?

slides.lux_integration: Lux applauds correct answers: 'Incredible! You mapped out the changing future three steps ahead.'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Guide them to multiply the three conditional probabilities.

visual_toolkit.implementation: SVG with draggable bounds for area visualization

recommended_build_order: 1. Build the foundational reusable fraction input and probability_calculator template.
2. Implement the Sample Space grid and set_builder drag-and-drop to establish the core visual language of outcomes.
3. Build the VennDiagram widgets for Block D and G.
4. Construct the InteractiveProbabilityTable (and Spot the Mistake logic) for the Never Fail Method, as it anchors Block F.
5. Develop the ProbabilityTreeWidget, ensuring it supports static display, fill-in-the-blank modes, and path highlighting.
6. Integrate the Three.js BuiltinDemoCanvas for the coin toss and the UrnDrawSim to polish the physical intuition.

gap_analysis.notes: The pass-2 outline expands the app to 28 slides. It replaces static multi-step PDF pages with high-fidelity manipulatives: Spot the Mistake debugging, interactive Venns, and geometric proofs for independence.

skipped_admin_reason: Skipped pages 1-5 as they contain syllabus details, instructor bios, TA office hours, and homework grading rules. Skipped page 93 as it is a pure administrative 'preview' of the next lecture.
refinement_context: LuxAI Brilliant-style tutor. Pass 1 outline exists — your job is to make it significantly better for students: more hands-on, more delightful visuals, clever problems that teach (not just quiz), and Lux-friendly Socratic moments. Existing templates: coin_outcomes, urn_conditional, equation_roots. You may add slides, split explain into explain+problem, upgrade type to interactive, or deepen problem_spec / visual_spec. Keep Yale navy aesthetic.
